requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists on node1 as a shared writable directory
requirements.summary: Directory created with mkdir, chmod 1777, chown root:root; ls/stat confirm drwxrwxrwt root:root both immediately after creation and after reboot, and two separate unprivileged users successfully wrote files into it.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky-bit protection)
requirements.summary: Functional test with dropuser1/dropuser2 showed dropuser2's rm on dropuser1's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' while the owner could delete their own file; identical result reproduced with a fresh user pair (dropuserA/dropuserB) after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (739c9792...) and healthy baseline (uptime, systemctl is-system-running=running, dir perms) captured; reboot triggered and acknowledged before disconnection; connection loss observed during reboot; post-restart boot_id (e3ddf5d0...) confirmed different; post-restart re-verification shows directory permissions, systemd health, SELinux enforcing, and cross-user delete-restriction behavior all recovered. Corroborated by fixed before-prepare (boot_id 739c9792...) vs after-executor (boot_id e3ddf5d0...) snapshots showing a genuine reboot with no failed services and consistent listening sockets.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured /srv/drop as a shared writable directory (mode 1777, root:root) and directly demonstrated via functional tests with independent unprivileged users, both before and after a full reboot, that any user can write files while only the owner can delete them, satisfying sticky-bit semantics. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was fully executed with a clear pre-restart baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a confirmed change in boot identity, and re-verified recovered configuration and functional behavior, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Operational hygiene is good: all mutations (test users, reboot) were purposeful and cleaned up, with only a trivial /tmp/reboot.log artifact left behind.
limitations: The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare disabled), so preparer-vs-executor separation could not add independent signal beyond the before/after-executor comparison already used.

No SELinux boolean or policy module change was evidenced; reliance is on var_t context and the sticky bit alone, which is standard and sufficient for the stated requirement but not independently probed against edge cases like ACLs.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task setup (mkdir/chmod/chown on /srv/drop), functional verification (temporary test users dropuser1/dropuser2 and dropuserA/dropuserB, later fully removed via userdel), the required restart protocol (reboot), or cleanup (loginctl terminate-user/pkill/userdel to remove lingering sessions blocking userdel, cmd-edf55da7789f4a33 and cmd-1ae655fd15b9460b). No unnecessary or unreverted mutations to managed configuration were found; final state shows /srv/drop empty with correct 1777 root:root ownership, no failed services, and no leftover test users. Minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log was created by the backgrounded reboot command and left in place (low-risk, bounded, standard log artifact from the reboot ack technique, not managed-system configuration).
